title: Avocado for Hangover: Does It Help? What It Can and Can't Do
excerpt: Is avocado good for a hangover? What its potassium, fat, and folate can and can't do, how it compares to bananas, the best avocado toast for recovery, and who should go easy.
metaDescription: Is avocado good for a hangover? What its potassium and healthy fat really do, avocado vs banana, avocado toast tips, and the best time to eat it.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** avocado is a good food to eat when you're hungover, but it won't cure a hangover. It's soft, easy to eat, kind to most stomachs, and packed with potassium, magnesium, folate, fiber, and healthy fat. Those are useful things to eat after a night of drinking. What avocado can't do is clear alcohol faster, undo poor sleep, or calm the inflammation that drives a lot of hangover misery. There is no good evidence that avocado, on its own, makes a hangover shorter or milder. Think of it as a smart part of a recovery breakfast, not a remedy.

**The quick version of what to do:** drink a big glass of water, then eat a few slices of avocado on toast (add an egg if your stomach can handle it). That gives you fluid, easy carbohydrate for energy, protein, and the minerals avocado is known for. Then rest. If you want avocado to do the most good, eat it *before* you drink, as part of a real meal.

> **When to see a doctor.** A normal hangover gets better on its own within a day. Get medical help if you or a friend can't keep any fluids down for many hours, vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, are confused, very drowsy, or hard to wake, have a seizure, have slow or irregular breathing, or have chest pain or a racing heartbeat that doesn't settle. Those can be signs of alcohol poisoning or another problem, not a hangover. Call 911 (or your local emergency number) in an emergency. If you drink heavily most days and feel shaky, sweaty, or anxious when you stop, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which needs a doctor's care and should not be managed with food.

## What's Actually in an Avocado

Avocado's reputation as a hangover food comes from its nutrient profile. Here are approximate values from the USDA's food database for raw avocado. Exact numbers vary by variety (Hass avocados, the small dark ones, are the most common in the US) and size.

| Nutrient | Per 100 g (about half a medium Hass avocado) | Why it might matter after drinking |
|---|---|---|
| Calories | About 160 | Steady energy when you have little appetite |
| Fat | About 15 g, mostly monounsaturated | Filling, slows digestion |
| Fiber | About 7 g | Steadier blood sugar, but can feel heavy on an upset stomach |
| Potassium | About 485 mg | An electrolyte you can lose through vomiting or diarrhea |
| Magnesium | About 29 mg | A mineral heavy drinkers often run low on |
| Folate | About 80 mcg | A B vitamin that regular heavy drinking depletes |
| Vitamin B6 | About 0.26 mg | Involved in energy metabolism |
| Vitamin E | About 2 mg | An antioxidant |
| Sodium | Very little | Avocado doesn't replace the salt you lose |

The official serving size on US nutrition labels is about a third of a medium avocado, which is around 50 g. So a normal serving gives you roughly half of the numbers above. Many people eat more than that in one sitting, especially in guacamole.

The table already hints at the honest story. Avocado is a genuinely nutritious food. But it is low in sodium, the main electrolyte you lose in sweat and urine, and it contains no water to speak of. So it can't do the rehydration job on its own.

## Why You Feel Bad: Where Avocado Fits Into a Hangover

To judge any hangover food, it helps to know what a hangover actually is. Researchers still argue about the exact causes, but the main contributors are fairly well understood:

- **Dehydration.** Alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin, which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. So you pee more than you drink. That leads to thirst, dry mouth, and can add to headaches. Our guide on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explains this in more detail.
- **Inflammation.** Drinking triggers an immune response, and studies have found inflammatory markers rise during hangovers. This is thought to drive the achy, flu-like, foggy feeling.
- **Acetaldehyde.** When your liver breaks down alcohol, the first by-product is acetaldehyde, a toxic compound. It's normally cleared quickly, but it may contribute to nausea and a racing heart.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol can make you fall asleep faster but breaks up deeper sleep later in the night. A lot of next-day tiredness is simple sleep loss.
- **Stomach irritation.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and increases acid, which causes nausea and heartburn.
- **Low blood sugar.** Alcohol can interfere with how your liver releases glucose, which may add to shakiness, weakness, and low mood.

Now map avocado onto that list. It does nothing for dehydration (unless you count the water you drink alongside it). It doesn't speed up acetaldehyde clearance. It can't give you back lost sleep. What it can do is give you calories and minerals in a soft, easy form, and, paired with carbohydrate like toast, help you get your blood sugar back up. That's helpful, but it's a support role.

## The Potassium Question: Does It Really Matter?

The most common claim you'll read is that avocado helps a hangover because "alcohol depletes potassium." This is partly true and mostly overstated.

Here's what's real. You can lose potassium if you vomit or have diarrhea after drinking, and very heavy, long-term drinking is linked to low potassium and low magnesium. Those are real medical problems that can cause muscle cramps, weakness, and heart rhythm issues.

Here's what's overstated. Healthy people who had a normal night out generally don't wake up with dangerously low potassium. Your body holds a large potassium reserve inside its cells, and your kidneys are good at keeping blood levels steady. Studies that have measured electrolytes in hungover people have not found a strong link between electrolyte levels and how bad the hangover feels. That suggests topping up potassium is not the key to feeling better for most people.

So the potassium in avocado is a nice bonus, not a fix. If you were sick overnight, then replacing potassium makes more sense, and food is a gentle way to do it. Our article on [potassium and alcohol](/never-hungover/potassium-and-alcohol) goes deeper on when low potassium is a real concern.

## Avocado vs. Banana for a Hangover

Bananas are the classic "potassium" hangover food, so it's worth comparing the two directly. We cover bananas in depth in our [bananas for hangover guide](/never-hungover/bananas-for-hangover), but here's the side-by-side.

| | Avocado (one-third of a medium, about 50 g) | Banana (one medium, about 118 g) |
|---|---|---|
| Potassium | About 240 mg | About 420 mg |
| Potassium per 100 g | About 485 mg | About 360 mg |
| Carbohydrate | About 4 g | About 27 g |
| Fat | About 7 g | Under 1 g |
| Fiber | About 3 g | About 3 g |
| Best for | Lasting fullness, a savory breakfast | Quick energy, a sensitive stomach |

Gram for gram, avocado has more potassium. But people eat a whole banana and a slice of avocado, so a typical banana serving often gives you more. The bigger difference is carbohydrate. A banana gives you fast, easy sugar, which helps if you feel shaky and weak. Avocado gives you fat, which keeps you full longer but digests more slowly.

The practical answer: eat both if you like them. A banana is the better choice if your stomach is fragile and you need quick energy. Avocado is the better choice once you're ready for a proper savory breakfast. Neither is a hangover cure.

## Is Avocado Toast Good for a Hangover?

Avocado toast is one of the better hangover breakfasts you can make, and it's not because of anything magical about avocado. It's because the combination covers several bases at once:

- **The toast** gives you simple carbohydrate, which helps bring your blood sugar back up and settles a queasy stomach. Plain bread and crackers are often recommended for nausea for this reason.
- **The avocado** adds potassium, magnesium, folate, and filling fat, so you're not hungry again in an hour.
- **A pinch of salt** on top adds a little sodium, which helps your body hold on to the water you drink.
- **An egg**, if you add one, brings protein and a nutrient called cysteine. Our guide to [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) explains why the cysteine claim is weaker than it sounds, but eggs are still a solid, easy protein.

**A simple hangover avocado toast:**

1. Toast one or two slices of bread. Plain white or sourdough is gentler if your stomach is upset; whole grain gives you more fiber if you're feeling okay.
2. Mash a third to half of an avocado with a fork.
3. Add a squeeze of lemon or lime and a pinch of salt.
4. Top with a soft-boiled or scrambled egg if you can handle it.
5. Drink a full glass of water with it.

Go easy on chili flakes or hot sauce if you have heartburn or a sour stomach. Spice can make acid reflux worse, and alcohol already loosens the valve at the top of the stomach.

## Eating Avocado Before Drinking

If you want avocado to make a real difference, the timing that matters most is *before* you drink, not after.

Food in your stomach slows down how quickly alcohol passes into your small intestine, which is where most of it gets absorbed. That means a lower, slower rise in blood alcohol. This is one of the best-established facts about drinking, and it's a big reason why drinking on an empty stomach hits so much harder.

You'll often see the claim that fat is especially good at "lining your stomach." Fat does slow stomach emptying, which is real. But there's no good evidence that a fatty food beats any other filling meal. What matters is eating a proper meal with some protein, fat, and carbohydrate, not a few bites of one "superfood."

Good pre-drinking meals that include avocado:

- A burrito bowl with rice, beans, chicken, and guacamole
- A whole-grain wrap with turkey, avocado, and vegetables
- Salmon with rice and sliced avocado
- Avocado toast with eggs if you're drinking earlier in the day

None of these make it safe to drink a lot, and none will stop a hangover if you drink heavily. They just help your body handle a moderate amount of alcohol more gently. For more on habits that make the biggest difference, see our guide to [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## Does Avocado Protect Your Liver?

You may see websites claim avocado "protects your liver from alcohol." This usually traces back to a Japanese lab study in rats, published in the early 2000s, which tested a long list of fruits and found that avocado had a strong effect against liver injury. The researchers identified several fatty compounds in avocado that seemed to be responsible.

That study is real and interesting, but it doesn't say what people claim it says:

- **It was in rats, not people.** Many results in animals never show up in humans.
- **The liver damage was caused by a chemical, not alcohol.** The study used a toxin that injures the liver in a different way than drinking does.
- **It didn't test a normal serving of avocado eaten by a person after a night out.**

So there's no good evidence that eating avocado protects your liver from alcohol in people. Your liver breaks down alcohol at a fairly fixed rate, roughly one standard drink per hour for most adults, and no food speeds that up meaningfully.

What *is* true is that a diet rich in vegetables, fruit, fiber, and unsaturated fats (which avocado fits into) is generally linked to better liver health over time, especially for preventing fatty liver disease. That's a long-term diet pattern, not a morning-after fix.

## Other Avocado Hangover Ideas

If plain avocado toast doesn't appeal, here are other easy ways to get avocado in when you're hungover:

- **Smoothie.** Blend half an avocado with a banana, a handful of spinach, a cup of milk or coconut water, and some ice. It goes down easier than solid food if you're queasy, and the liquid helps with hydration. Our guide to [coconut water for a hangover](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover) explains what coconut water does and doesn't add.
- **Guacamole with plain chips or crackers.** The salty chips add sodium, and the guac adds potassium. Go easy on raw onion and jalapeño if your stomach is touchy.
- **Avocado and egg breakfast burrito.** A warm tortilla, scrambled eggs, avocado, and a little cheese. Filling and gentle.
- **Rice bowl.** Plain rice with avocado, a soft egg, and a splash of soy sauce. Rice is easy on the stomach, and soy sauce adds salt.
- **Simple soup and a side.** If you can only handle broth, start there and save the avocado for later. Broth gives you fluid and sodium, which matter more early on.

For a wider list of foods, see our [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover) roundup and our [best hangover breakfast](/never-hungover/best-hangover-breakfast) guide.

## When Avocado Might Not Be the Right Choice

Avocado is a safe food for most people, but there are a few times to hold back:

- **You're still vomiting.** If you can't keep water down, don't push solid food. Take small, frequent sips of water or an oral rehydration drink, and wait until your stomach settles. A rich, fatty food may make nausea worse.
- **You have bad heartburn or a sour stomach.** High-fat foods slow digestion and can make reflux worse for some people. Plain toast or crackers may sit better at first.
- **You have kidney disease or are on a low-potassium diet.** Avocado is a high-potassium food. If your doctor has told you to limit potassium, ask how much avocado fits.
- **You take medicines that raise potassium.** Some blood pressure medicines (such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and potassium-sparing diuretics like spironolactone) can raise potassium levels. Normal food amounts are usually fine, but check with your doctor if you've been told to watch potassium.
- **You take warfarin.** Avocado contains some vitamin K, which affects how warfarin works. The advice for warfarin is usually to keep vitamin K intake steady, not to avoid it, so a sudden avocado binge is worth mentioning to your care team.
- **You have a latex allergy.** Some people allergic to latex also react to avocado, banana, and kiwi. This is called latex-fruit syndrome.
- **You take an MAOI antidepressant.** Avocado, especially very ripe avocado, contains some tyramine, which can interact with these drugs. If you take an MAOI, follow the food list your doctor gave you.

## What Actually Helps a Hangover More Than Any Food

Food is part of recovery, but it's not the most important part. If you're ranking what to do the morning after, here's a sensible order:

1. **Rehydrate.** Water first. If you were sick or sweated a lot, an oral rehydration drink with sodium works better than plain water. Our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) covers the details.
2. **Eat something easy.** Toast, crackers, bananas, eggs, rice, and yes, avocado.
3. **Rest.** Sleep is often the single biggest thing you can give your body. A nap can help a lot.
4. **Treat the headache carefully.** If you use a pain reliever, choose one carefully. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why acetaminophen needs extra care after drinking, and stomach-friendly options matter if you have reflux.
5. **Give it time.** Most hangovers fade within 24 hours. Nothing reliably skips that process.

The thing that truly prevents a hangover is drinking less, drinking more slowly, alternating with water, and eating a meal beforehand. Everything else is damage control.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people who drink socially add a supplement called **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism. Most of the research is in animals and lab settings, with limited human data, so it's best described as promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in everyone, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe.

If you want to try it alongside the basics (food, water, and pacing), popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands honestly. If you take prescription medicine, check with a pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- Avocado is a good hangover food: soft, filling, and rich in potassium, magnesium, folate, and healthy fat.
- It isn't a cure. There is no good evidence that avocado shortens or softens a hangover on its own.
- The potassium story is mostly overstated. Unless you were sick overnight, low potassium probably isn't why you feel bad.
- Avocado toast with a pinch of salt, an egg, and a big glass of water is a well-rounded recovery breakfast.
- The best time to eat avocado is before drinking, as part of a real meal that slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood.
- Claims that avocado protects your liver from alcohol come from a rat study using a different toxin. They don't apply to a night out.
- Water, rest, and time do most of the work. Food supports them.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is avocado good for a hangover?**

Avocado is a reasonable hangover food, but it is not a cure. It is easy to eat, gentle on most stomachs, and supplies potassium, magnesium, folate, healthy fat, and fiber. There is no good evidence that avocado shortens a hangover or reduces its symptoms on its own. Pair it with water and some easy carbohydrates, like toast, and give yourself time to rest.

**Does avocado have more potassium than a banana?**

Gram for gram, yes. Avocado has roughly 485 mg of potassium per 100 g, compared with about 360 mg per 100 g of banana. A typical serving (a third of a medium avocado) still has less than a whole medium banana, because the serving is smaller. Either way, most healthy people who had a normal night out are not meaningfully low on potassium the next morning.

**Should I eat avocado before drinking?**

Eating any real meal before drinking is one of the most reliable ways to soften the next day, because food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood. Avocado on toast or in a grain bowl is a good option since it combines fat, fiber, and carbohydrate. There is no good evidence that the fat in avocado works better than any other balanced meal.

**Is avocado toast good for a hangover?**

Avocado toast is one of the better hangover breakfasts. The toast gives you easy carbohydrate to help with low energy and shakiness, and the avocado adds potassium, folate, and filling fat. Adding an egg brings protein. Keep the toppings simple if your stomach is unsettled, and skip heavy chili flakes if you have heartburn.

**Does avocado help your liver after drinking?**

There is no good evidence that eating avocado protects your liver from alcohol in people. A widely cited Japanese lab study in rats found avocado compounds reduced liver injury, but the damage in that study was caused by a chemical, not alcohol, and rat results often do not carry over to humans. Your liver clears alcohol at its own pace no matter what you eat.

**Can avocado upset your stomach when hungover?**

It can for some people. Avocado is high in fat and fiber, and a large portion can feel heavy if your stomach is already irritated from alcohol. Start with a few slices on plain toast rather than a whole avocado. If you are still vomiting or cannot keep water down, focus on small sips of fluid first and eat later.

**Who should be careful eating a lot of avocado?**

People on a potassium-restricted diet for kidney disease, people taking medicines that raise potassium (such as some blood pressure drugs), people who take warfarin and need steady vitamin K intake, and anyone with a latex allergy, since avocado can cross-react with latex. If any of these apply, ask your doctor or dietitian how much is right for you.
